title: Biomolecules overview
examples: What is the basic building block of a protein?
Can you explain the difference between lipids and carbohydrates?

explain.say: Today we are learning about biomolecules in living things. These are large biological molecules essential for life.
First we look at carbohydrates. These are important for quick energy for our bodies. A simple example is starch found in potatoes.
Next we study lipids. These are mostly known for storing long-term energy in our bodies. A common example is the fat found in nuts.
Proteins are very important for structure and function in cells. Their monomers are called amino acids. Think about the structure of hair.
Finally we have nucleic acids. These molecules carry the instructions for life. DNA is the most famous example of this molecule.
In everyday life, when you eat bread, you get carbohydrates for quick energy. The body breaks down the starch into glucose to use.

faq.q: What is the difference between a monomer and a polymer?
faq.a: A monomer is a small, single repeating unit. A polymer is a large molecule made up of many linked monomers.
asks: What are the building blocks of biomolecules?
Can you give an example of a simple unit forming a complex one?

faq.q: Are all fats the same, or are there different types?
faq.a: Fats are classified by their fatty acid chains, such as saturated or unsaturated. This affects how solid or liquid they are at room temperature.
asks: What makes some oils solid and others liquid?
Do all lipids behave the same way?

faq.q: How does the body know which protein to build?
faq.a: The instructions for building specific proteins are stored in the DNA molecule. This process is called gene expression.
asks: Where are the protein blueprints kept?

faq.q: What is the main difference between DNA and RNA?
faq.a: DNA is usually found in the nucleus and carries the permanent instructions. RNA is often involved in carrying out those instructions temporarily.
asks: Are DNA and RNA the same?
What is the role of RNA in biology?

faq.q: Can I get energy from lipids, or only from carbohydrates?
faq.a: You can get energy from all three main groups: carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins. Lipids provide a very concentrated source of energy.
asks: Which biomolecule stores the most energy?
Is protein energy source only for muscle?

facts: Carbohydrates are polymers made of many simple sugar units called monosaccharides.
Lipids include fats, oils, and waxes, which are excellent for long-term energy storage.
Proteins are polymers formed by linking amino acids together in specific sequences.
Nucleic acids, like DNA, store and transmit the hereditary information in all living things.

quiz.say: What is the monomer unit of a protein?
quiz.why: Proteins are long chains built by linking individual amino acids together.

wrong.1: Glucose is the monomer for carbohydrates, not proteins.
wrong.2: Nucleotides are the monomers for nucleic acids like DNA.
wrong.3: Fatty acids are components of lipids, not the main building block of protein.

quiz.say: Which biomolecule is primarily responsible for carrying genetic instructions?
quiz.why: DNA, a type of nucleic acid, holds the blueprint for life in the cell.

wrong.0: Proteins carry out functions, but DNA carries the instructions for those functions.
wrong.1: Carbohydrates are mainly used for immediate energy supply.
wrong.2: Lipids are mainly used for long-term energy storage and cell membranes.

quiz.say: If a cell needs immediate energy, which biomolecule would it break down first?
quiz.why: Carbohydrates like glucose are broken down relatively quickly to release usable energy.

wrong.0: Nucleic acids are primarily informational molecules and not a major energy source.
wrong.2: Proteins are usually reserved for structure, and breaking them down for energy is a last resort.
wrong.3: Lipids store energy for the long term, making them slower to access for immediate needs.
